name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,582

clue.text: Morse perhaps starts to criticise other detectives' evidence

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: Inspector Morse finds fault with the evidence gathered by rival detectives.
explanation.walkthrough: Morse is the famous TV detective, which makes the clue look like police business; here it means the telegraph alphabet of dots and dashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse is one example of a signalling system that turns letters into dots and dashes, which is a kind of cipher or encoding.

clue.text: A bicycle's broken - no riding in this state

indicators.note: something broken has its parts out of place, so the preceding letters are disordered

blocks.note: both words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: A cyclist's bike is broken, so they cannot go riding while it is in this condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riding' is slang for having sex, so the state of no riding is sexual abstinence.
explanation.definitionFit: Celibacy is the condition of abstaining from sex, and riding is vulgar slang for sexual intercourse.

clue.text: Whimsical nobleman upset by lake

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word is read bottom to top

blocks.note: a lord is a nobleman
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A fanciful aristocrat is distressed beside a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Droll humour is quirky and amusing in an odd way, which matches the sense of whimsical or fanciful.

clue.text: A dish - vindaloo?

blocks.note: first meaning: an attractive person, informally called a dish
second meaning: a fiery curry, something with a lot of chilli heat

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as though vindaloo is offered as an example of a dish; instead 'dish' is slang for a sexy person, and both halves share one phrase. Vindaloo is a very spicy curry, a staple of British curry houses.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for a sexually attractive person and also literally describes spicy, fiery food.

clue.text: Someone experienced and supporting former husband

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporting piece sits beneath, so it is written after the rest

blocks.note: old means former, as in an old flame
H is the abbreviation for husband
taken as written

explanation.surface: A veteran is still helping out his ex-husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like a joining word, but it is a piece of the answer placed under the others.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran with long practice at something is described with this idiom for a seasoned expert.

clue.text: Place for rhino attracting interest?

blocks.note: surface reading: a zoo enclosure where a rhinoceros draws curious visitors
setter's reading: rhino is old British slang for money, and interest is what a bank pays on deposits

explanation.walkthrough: Rhino is old British slang for cash; interest is the bank's payment, not curiosity.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank deposit where cash is kept and earns interest over time is exactly this sort of account.

clue.text: Tuna swimming around northern river? Weird

indicators.note: a fish swimming moves about freely, so its letters are shifted into a new order
around means surrounding, so the jumbled fish encloses the next letter

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for northern
the Ural is a river flowing from the Ural Mountains to the Caspian Sea

explanation.surface: A tuna swimming in a northern river would be a strange sight.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the setter's tuna has strayed far from salt water.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unnatural is abnormal and strange, outside the usual run of things, which is what weird means.

clue.text: Break from female trouble

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female
to ail is to trouble, as in what ails you

explanation.surface: Someone takes a break from the trouble caused by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' looks like a noun for a rest; it is the verb, as when a machine stops working.
explanation.definitionFit: When a machine or engine breaks down it stops working, and that is what the verb fail means here.

clue.text: Replacing waste ground for health resorts

indicators.note: ground means milled or crushed, so the letters are reduced and remade in another order

blocks.note: both words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: Wasteland is redeveloped to build health spas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste ground' reads as derelict land; 'ground' is the signal and 'waste' part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Spa towns such as Bath, where visitors took the mineral waters for their health, were known by this old phrase.

clue.text: Help father to get over bad habit

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting over means flipping upward, so the word is read from the bottom

blocks.note: da is an informal word for dad
a vice is a bad habit

explanation.surface: Dad tries to help his child kick a bad habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Counsel or guidance offered to someone is a form of assistance, so the noun can stand for help.

clue.text: Dali carved onion - surreal artist

indicators.note: something surreal is bizarrely distorted, so the preceding letters are jumbled into a strange new order

blocks.note: all three words are used letter for letter

explanation.surface: Salvador Dali sculpts an onion, and the result is a surreal work of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carved' looks like the anagram signal and 'surreal artist' like a description of Dali; in fact 'carved' is part of the letters, 'surreal' is the signal, and the artist is a different painter entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci was the Renaissance painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, so he is an artist.

clue.text: She might display attitude in Romeo and Juliet

definitions.text: She might display attitude in Romeo and Juliet

blocks.note: surface reading: a stroppy girl, perhaps a teenage Juliet, showing defiance
setter's reading: an attitude is a classical ballet pose on one leg, and Romeo and Juliet is Prokofiev's ballet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Attitude' suggests sulky behaviour, but in ballet it is a position with one leg raised behind and bent; Romeo and Juliet here is the ballet, not the play.
explanation.definitionFit: A female dancer performing in the ballet version of Romeo and Juliet would hold the pose called an attitude.

clue.text: Acorns, perhaps, out of one's tree

blocks.note: first meaning: acorns are an example of hard-shelled tree fruit
second meaning: an idiom for crazy

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures acorns falling out of an oak; 'out of one's tree' is in fact an idiom for being mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Acorns are oak fruits with shells, and the word is also informal slang for crazy or insane.

clue.text: Marry groom and fashionable bride, finally

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the preceding word, so only its closing letter is used

blocks.note: to groom hair is to comb it
in fashion is in
the last letter of bride

explanation.surface: A wedding scene: the groom and his stylish bride are getting married at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' and 'bride' look like the couple but are a verb for tidying hair and a letter source.
explanation.definitionFit: To marry two things is to join or unite them, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Quiet person chops Cheddar cheese

blocks.note: a timid, quiet person is called a mouse
chops and trap are both slang for the mouth

explanation.surface: A shy person cuts up some cheddar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chops' reads as a verb for cutting, but it is slang for the mouth. In Britain, cheap mild cheddar is nicknamed after what it is used to bait.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang names bland, cheap cheese after the device it would bait, so a block of supermarket cheddar qualifies.

clue.text: Fancy gentleman wearing flower

indicators.note: whatever is wearing something is enclosed by it, so the gentleman sits inside the flower

blocks.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Dee is a river in Wales, Scotland and England
the form of address for a gentleman

explanation.surface: A dapper gentleman wears a flower in his buttonhole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the crossword trick for a river, something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy something is to want or long for it, and as a noun a fancy is a wish or craving.

clue.text: One who fights with the French king after all others

indicators.note: after places the words before it behind the one that follows

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
the rest means all the others
le is French for the
R is for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A warrior battles alongside the French monarch while everyone else hangs back.
explanation.definitionFit: A grappler in the ring is a sportsman who fights opponents by throwing and pinning them.

clue.text: The woman traps animal, reflecting need for food

indicators.note: a reflection shows things mirror-wise, so the animal's name is read backwards
to trap something is to hold it inside, so the woman encloses the animal

blocks.note: the pronoun for a woman
a wildebeest, the crossword's favourite animal

explanation.surface: A woman catches an animal for her dinner, thinking about how hungry she is.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the feeling of wanting to eat, a physical craving or appetite when the stomach is empty.

clue.text: Bond hit right in belly

indicators.note: in places the letter for right inside the word for belly

blocks.note: a rap is a sharp blow
a pot belly; pot is slang for a paunch
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: James Bond punches a villain squarely in the stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' suggests 007, but here it is a connection between people.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapport is a close, harmonious relationship, a connection or tie of understanding between people.

clue.text: Lay awake initially beset by terrible ulcers

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word before it
terrible suggests something wrecked, so the letters of the following word are rearranged
to be beset is to be surrounded, so the single letter goes inside the jumble

blocks.note: the first letter of awake
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lies awake at night, kept up by painful ulcers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' looks like a verb, past tense of lie; it is the adjective meaning not of the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay people are those not ordained in a church, so the adjective means worldly, non-religious or non-clerical.

clue.text: Mean pop star - my money is missing

indicators.note: missing means absent, so the named letter is taken out of the word

blocks.note: Sting is the singer, formerly of The Police
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: A tight-fisted pop star complains that his cash has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The pop star is the singer Sting; removing M from my leaves Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean in the British sense is ungenerous with money, tight-fisted and unwilling to spend.

clue.text: Go with Liberal Prime Minister

blocks.note: to go is a euphemism for urinating
the standard abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A politician joins a Liberal Prime Minister in coalition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal Prime Minister' reads as one phrase, but Liberal only gives a letter; Robert Peel was in fact a Conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Robert Peel served twice as Britain's leader in the nineteenth century and founded the modern police force.

clue.text: I soon gasp fighting this?

indicators.note: things that are fighting are in a tangled melee, so the preceding letters are mixed up

blocks.note: all three words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: A soldier in battle finds himself choking almost at once.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the letter mix and the picture: a soldier fighting in a chemical attack quickly struggles for breath.
explanation.definitionFit: Chlorine and mustard weapons of the First World War made soldiers in the trenches choke and struggle for breath.

clue.text: Booze thrown up, with European revealing stomach contents

indicators.note: in a down clue, thrown up means sent upward, so the word is read from the bottom

blocks.note: grog is alcoholic drink, originally rum and water
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A drunk vomits after too much alcohol, and a European sees what was in his stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrown up' fits the vomiting picture but signals the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: In older usage the word means what has been swallowed, as in one's gorge rising with disgust or nausea.

clue.text: View model scratching bottom

indicators.note: scratching means striking out, and the bottom of a down entry is its last letter, which goes

blocks.note: an ideal is a model to follow

explanation.surface: A fashion model is seen scratching her backside.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion or way of thinking about something can be called a view, as in having an idea of it.

clue.text: BBC head maybe recreating older broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast also means scattered widely, as seed is, so the preceding letters are dispersed into a new order

blocks.note: both words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: The BBC's boss is accused of repeating old programmes on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the BBC so well it looks like part of the picture, but it signals the letter mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief executive of the British Broadcasting Corporation holds this title, so the BBC's head is an example.

clue.text: Suitable place to carry parrot? On the contrary

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another
this flips the roles just described, so the parrot does the carrying rather than the place

blocks.note: to parrot or ape is to mimic
to posit is to put or place in position

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a place is suitable for carrying a pet parrot, and is told the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'place' and 'parrot' are verbs here, and 'On the contrary' swaps which word holds which.
explanation.definitionFit: An apposite remark is apt and well-suited to the occasion, so the adjective means appropriate or fitting.

clue.text: Does perhaps run after girl

indicators.note: after places the word before it behind the one that follows

blocks.note: Dee is a girl's name
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone runs off after a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like the verb do; it is the plural of doe, a female deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Does are female animals of the antlered family, so they are examples of the plural animal named here.
